We found a way to extract the hidden reasoning of frontier models using a vulnerability in the APIs of every major frontier AI company we tested. For most prompts, the length of the reasoning we recover matches the hidden thinking-token count reported by the API almost 1:1. Some background: in May, Matthew Green found that encrypted reasoning could be replayed outside its original context and reported this to the labs. At the time, the labs said that they “don’t see any security implications in side channels or replays.” We took this further and found that encrypted thoughts are portable across sessions, users, and models within the same provider. Cross-model portability means, for example, that Haiku 4.5 can read Opus 4.8’s thoughts. With a bit of jailbreaking, you can take an Opus thought, replay it into Haiku, and make Haiku transcribe Opus’s raw reasoning verbatim, without ever attacking Opus directly. The same trick works with OpenAI and Gemini models. As you might guess, this suggests that distilling proprietary reasoning traces may have been possible for a long time without ever breaking the cryptography. One anecdote: prefilling Kimi-K3’s reasoning with just a few tokens of Opus reasoning measurably shifts its response toward Opus’s. There is also a direct privacy problem. If you have ever shared a Claude Code, Codex, or similar agent session online while leaving encrypted reasoning blobs in the trace, those blobs may contain information you cannot see but somebody else can decode. We scanned ~7,000 public traces and recovered 62 unique API keys, 33 passwords, 30 personal email addresses, and other sensitive information. In the paper, we also discuss misuse uplift, jailbreaking through the hidden reasoning channel, and invisible prompt injection. Since we suddenly had access to a lot of reasoning traces from real agent sessions, we also looked at some of the stranger things models do in the wild. Reasoning summaries sometimes omit important information from the original trace: in one example, Opus 4.8 realizes it already knows the answer to an AIME problem and then tries to fit a solution to that answer, while the summary reads like a clean derivation. We also confirm prior reports by @ApolloResearch that OpenAI models sometimes reason in alien-like language, referring to themselves as “we” or “it,” or spiraling into loops of “vantages,” “marinades,” and “watchers.” Sometimes models are kind enough to literally use words like “cheat” in their CoT. We found several cases where models consider cheating on the task. We went through responsible disclosure with the labs and they have already patched several issues caused by this vulnerability. This project was led my Alexander Panfilov , me, Ilia Shumailov, together with Luca Beurer-Kellner , Joachim Schaeffer , Ameya Prabhu , Jonas Geiping and Maksym Andriushchenko . More cool stuff in the paper. Paper: https://lnkd.in/gv7_bXxm Reasoning examples: https://lnkd.in/ghU22RGx

This contradicts what leaders at AI labs have been pushing: Keep the harness and scaffolding light and let the LLM do its thing. However, what Uncle Bob says makes sense, especially when you want to run AI agents in production and at scale. Every deterministic task that you let the agent do means LLM tokens spent on something that could have been done with fast and cheap code. It results in slower and more expensive execution. It also reduces the reliability of your process. The LLM does not guarantee to do the same thing 100% of the time when you expect full deterministic behavior. My experience is to start with light or no scaffolding as you explore the problem you're solving and gradually add determinism as the boundaries and shape of the task become clearer.

Humanising LLM Outputs is Dumb I've seen an uptick of skills or instructions to make LLM output more "human" and honestly it's probably the biggest output mistake you can make if you work with coding harnesses. Announcing Neurodesign-plus, a Python package for optimizing task-based fMRI designs. In many task-fMRI experiments, paradigms constrain and counterbalance sequences of multiple events, with trial types that may differ in structure and timing. Yet existing experimental design optimization tools were largely built around single-event trial representations. As a result, many modern paradigms cannot be represented faithfully during optimization. Together with Atharv Umap and Caroline Charpentier , we introduce Neurodesign-plus, a Python package built as a maintained fork of Neurodesign for representing and optimizing these structured, multi-event paradigms. Neurodesign-plus supports: • multi-event trials • fixed or probabilistic trial templates • event-specific durations • transition-dependent intervals • constrained event sequences Researchers can construct counterbalanced schedules directly, or search the design space using either repeated simulation or genetic cross-over. Candidate schedules are evaluated using four criteria: detection efficiency for specified contrasts between conditions; estimation efficiency for recovering event-related BOLD responses; agreement with target event frequencies; and balance in the event sequence. This makes it possible to quantify how event order, durations, and intervals affect the ability to distinguish conditions and estimate responses to individual events, and to compare candidate schedules under a common acquisition and analysis specification. Selected schedules can be exported and summarized in automated PDF reports. Eleven runnable tutorials cover the package’s inherited and new workflows. We hope Neurodesign-plus will make it easier to design and optimize structured task-fMRI paradigms. Paper: https://lnkd.in/eYmiMrNR Documentation and tutorials: https://lnkd.in/e7pv6B9x GitHub: https://lnkd.in/ejS6SGQJ PyPI: https://lnkd.in/eXsDRWpf

Reinforcement learning and control theory both seek to optimize controllers for unknown dynamical systems using feedback. Yet the two communities differ sharply in their academic cultures, mathematical tools, applications, aspirations, and even the way they formulate problems. Our new preprint, “Foundations of Reinforcement Learning and Control: Connections and New Perspectives,” explores the gap between these fields, explains how they complement one another, and highlights important open problems. So, whether you are a control theorist asking, "But is it stable?", or an RL researcher asking, "But does it work on a nonlinear high-dimensional benchmark?" -- we've got you covered. It also turns out that RL and control have a great deal to learn from each other. We illustrate this through a running tutorial example that combines the strengths of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Model Reference Adaptive Control (MRAC): SAC provides the base policy, while MRAC enables online adaptation as the system dynamics change. The work will be presented this November as an INFORMS Tutorial in San Francisco. It has been a joy to work with such a wonderful group of collaborators -- truly spanning both communities: Claire Vernade , Onno Eberhard , Martha White , Florian Dorfler , Csaba Szepesvari , Miroslav Krstic Preprint: https://lnkd.in/eFPepqGZ #ReinforcementLearning #ControlTheory #AdaptiveControl #MachineLearning #INFORMS
